title: Molecular Diagnostics and Laboratory Quality Management
description: Nucleic acid extraction, PCR and its variants, sequencing, molecular diagnosis of infections and genetic disorders, biosafety, and laboratory quality management systems.

topics.title: Nucleic Acid Extraction and PCR
topics.summary: Extraction methods, PCR principles, components, cycling and contamination control.

notes.b: Molecular testing starts with good-quality nucleic acid. Extraction steps: cell lysis (detergents, proteinase K, chaotropic salts such as guanidinium), separation of nucleic acid from proteins and debris (organic phenol–chloroform extraction, silica spin columns — nucleic acid binds silica in high salt and elutes in low-salt buffer, or magnetic beads for automation), washing and elution. RNA is labile (RNases are ubiquitous) — use RNase-free materials and stabilisers, and process or freeze quickly. Quality and quantity are checked by spectrophotometry (A260/A280 ratio about 1.8 for pure DNA and 2.0 for RNA; A260/A230 detects salt/organic contamination) or fluorometry. Specimen types include EDTA blood (not heparin — inhibits PCR), swabs in viral transport medium, sputum, tissue and dried blood spots (used for infant HIV testing in Nigeria).

notes.b: The polymerase chain reaction (Kary Mullis, 1983) amplifies a target DNA sequence exponentially. Components: template, two primers flanking the target, thermostable DNA polymerase (Taq from Thermus aquaticus), dNTPs, Mg²⁺ (cofactor) and buffer. Each cycle: denaturation (~94–95 °C), annealing (~50–65 °C, depending on primer melting temperature), extension (~72 °C); 30–40 cycles theoretically give 2^n copies. Products are detected by agarose gel electrophoresis with DNA stain against a molecular weight ladder. Contamination (especially amplicon carry-over) causes false positives — prevented by physically separate pre- and post-PCR areas with unidirectional workflow, dedicated equipment and filter tips, UNG/dUTP systems, and no-template (negative) controls in every run. Inhibitors (heme, heparin, humic acids) cause false negatives — detected with internal (amplification) controls.

topics.title: Real-time PCR and Advanced Molecular Methods
topics.summary: qPCR and RT-PCR, viral load, isothermal amplification, sequencing and point-of-care molecular tests.

notes.b: Real-time (quantitative) PCR monitors amplification each cycle using fluorescence — non-specific DNA-binding dyes (SYBR Green; melt curve analysis checks specificity) or sequence-specific probes (TaqMan hydrolysis probes with reporter and quencher dyes). The cycle threshold (Ct) is the cycle at which fluorescence crosses the threshold; lower Ct means more starting target. Quantification uses standard curves of known concentrations; efficiency of 90–110% is acceptable. Reverse-transcription PCR (RT-PCR) first converts RNA to cDNA (reverse transcriptase) — used for HIV viral load, hepatitis C RNA, SARS-CoV-2 and Lassa virus detection (NCDC network laboratories). Multiplex PCR detects several targets in one reaction. Advantages: closed-tube (less contamination), fast and quantitative.

Cartridge-based automated platforms (GeneXpert — Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra detects Mycobacterium tuberculosis and rifampicin resistance in about 2 hours; also HIV viral load and early infant diagnosis) have transformed diagnosis in Nigeria, where over a thousand machines support the TB programme. Isothermal methods (LAMP — loop-mediated isothermal amplification) amplify at a single temperature without a thermocycler. Line probe assays (e.g. for TB drug resistance) hybridise amplicons to probes on strips. Sequencing: Sanger (chain termination, dideoxynucleotides — accurate for single genes) and next-generation sequencing (massively parallel — whole genomes, genomic surveillance of outbreaks; e.g. Lassa, mpox and SARS-CoV-2 sequencing at the African Centre of Excellence for Genomics of Infectious Diseases (ACEGID), Ede, and NCDC). Nanopore sequencers are portable for field use.

topics.title: Molecular Diagnosis of Genetic and Haematological Disorders
topics.summary: Sickle cell genotyping, prenatal and newborn diagnosis, cancer molecular testing and pharmacogenomics.

notes.b: Nigeria has the world's largest burden of sickle cell disease (over 150,000 affected births yearly). Diagnosis by haemoglobin electrophoresis (cellulose acetate at alkaline pH), isoelectric focusing and HPLC (quantifies HbF, HbA2, HbS) is complemented by DNA methods (PCR–restriction enzyme analysis — the sickle mutation GAG→GTG in codon 6 of the β-globin gene abolishes a DdeI/MstII site; allele-specific PCR). Newborn screening uses dried blood spots with IEF or HPLC, and point-of-care lateral-flow tests (e.g. HemoTypeSC, Sickle SCAN). Prenatal diagnosis via chorionic villus sampling (10–13 weeks) or amniocentesis, with DNA analysis, is available in a few Nigerian centres; preimplantation genetic testing is offered by some IVF clinics. Other applications: G6PD genotyping, thalassaemia mutations, cystic fibrosis panels and karyotyping/FISH/microarrays for chromosomal disorders (Down syndrome — trisomy 21).

Molecular oncology detects translocations and mutations guiding diagnosis and targeted therapy: BCR-ABL1 (Philadelphia chromosome t(9;22) in chronic myeloid leukaemia — monitored by quantitative RT-PCR during imatinib therapy), JAK2 V617F (myeloproliferative neoplasms), PML-RARA (acute promyelocytic leukaemia — treated with ATRA), MYC translocation (Burkitt lymphoma), EGFR mutations (lung adenocarcinoma — EGFR inhibitors), KRAS (colorectal cancer — predicts lack of benefit from anti-EGFR antibodies), BRCA1/2 (hereditary breast and ovarian cancer — PARP inhibitors) and HER2 amplification. Liquid biopsy detects circulating tumour DNA in plasma. Pharmacogenomics tailors drugs to genotype: CYP2B6 variants (common in Africans — high efavirenz levels and CNS side effects), CYP2C19 (clopidogrel), HLA-B*5701 (abacavir), TPMT (thiopurines) and G6PD (primaquine, dapsone).

topics.title: Biosafety and Biosecurity
topics.summary: Risk groups, biosafety levels, biological safety cabinets, and handling high-consequence pathogens.

notes.b: Microorganisms are classified into risk groups 1–4 by pathogenicity, transmissibility and availability of treatment/prevention: RG1 (unlikely to cause disease), RG2 (moderate individual risk — most clinical bacteria, HBV, HIV in routine diagnostic work), RG3 (high individual risk, low community risk — M. tuberculosis culture, Brucella, yellow fever virus), RG4 (high individual and community risk, no treatment — Ebola, Marburg, Lassa virus under some classifications). Biosafety levels (BSL-1 to BSL-4) specify practices, safety equipment and facility design; WHO's 2020 Laboratory Biosafety Manual promotes a risk-based approach (core requirements, heightened control measures, maximum containment). Nigeria has BSL-3 laboratories (e.g. NCDC National Reference Laboratory Abuja, Irrua Specialist Teaching Hospital — Lassa fever) and TB culture laboratories.

Biological safety cabinets (BSCs): Class I (protects operator and environment, not product), Class II (the most common — HEPA-filtered downflow and inflow protect operator, product and environment; used for TB, viral cultures and molecular work) and Class III (glove box, totally enclosed — RG4 agents). A BSC is not a chemical fume hood. BSCs need annual certification and correct use (work in the centre, avoid rapid arm movement, don't block grilles, UV lamps are not a substitute for disinfection). Good microbiological technique: no mouth pipetting, no eating in the lab, lab coats and gloves, hand hygiene, safe sharps handling, decontamination (autoclaving at 121 °C for 15 minutes, 0.5% hypochlorite for spills), spill kits, triple packaging for specimen transport (UN3373 Category B; Category A UN2814 for high-consequence pathogens), and incident reporting. Biosecurity protects dangerous pathogens from theft or misuse. Staff should be vaccinated (hepatitis B) and have PEP access.

topics.title: Laboratory Quality Management Systems
topics.summary: Quality essentials, QC statistics, EQA, accreditation (SLIPTA, ISO 15189) and LIS.

notes.b: A quality management system covers the 12 quality system essentials (WHO/CLSI): organisation, personnel, equipment, purchasing and inventory, process control, information management, documents and records, occurrence management, assessment, process improvement, customer service, and facilities and safety. Errors occur most often in the pre-analytical phase (patient identification, labelling, collection, transport — about 60–70%), then post-analytical (reporting, transcription) and analytical phases. Document control ensures current SOPs. The Stepwise Laboratory Quality Improvement Process Towards Accreditation (SLIPTA — WHO AFRO) grades laboratories from 0 to 5 stars, and the SLMTA training programme supports improvement; many Nigerian laboratories have progressed through it to ISO 15189 accreditation (e.g. via SANAS or other bodies). The Medical Laboratory Science Council of Nigeria (MLSCN) regulates laboratories and practitioners.

Internal quality control (IQC) runs control materials of known values with patient samples; results are plotted on Levey–Jennings charts (mean ± 1, 2, 3 SD) and interpreted with Westgard rules: 1-2s (warning), 1-3s (reject — random error), 2-2s (two consecutive beyond 2 SD same side — systematic error), R-4s (range between two controls > 4 SD — random error), 4-1s and 10x (systematic shifts/trends). Accuracy (closeness to the true value) differs from precision (reproducibility, measured by coefficient of variation — CV = SD/mean × 100). External quality assessment (EQA/proficiency testing) sends unknown samples from an external provider and compares results with peers. Qualitative tests (e.g. HIV rapid tests) use positive and negative controls. Laboratory information systems (LIS) reduce transcription errors, track turnaround time and support audits. Method validation/verification checks precision, accuracy, linearity, reference ranges and limits of detection.
